title: Perl tutorial: scalars, arrays, hashes and regular expressions — cv.cm
description: Learn Perl step by step: run a script, scalars, arrays and hashes, control flow, subroutines, references, regular expressions, die and eval, and a log parser.
answer: Perl is a dynamic scripting language created by Larry Wall in 1987, best known for text processing and powerful built-in regular expressions. It is preinstalled on most Unix systems and used for system administration, log processing and bioinformatics. This page covers running Perl, scalars, arrays and hashes, control flow, subroutines, references, regular expressions and error handling with die and eval.

sections.h: What Perl is and what it is used for
body: Perl is a high-level, dynamically typed language created by Larry Wall in 1987. It was designed for text processing and report generation, and it became known as the glue language of Unix system administration and early web development. Perl's regular expressions were so influential that many other languages adopted a "Perl-compatible" regex syntax.

Today Perl is used for system administration scripts, log and text processing, bioinformatics, legacy web applications and one-line command-line filters. It is preinstalled on most Linux and Unix systems. CPAN, the Comprehensive Perl Archive Network, hosts a very large collection of reusable modules. This tutorial covers Perl 5; the language once called Perl 6 is now a separate language named Raku.
Check that Perl is installed with `perl -v`. On Windows, Strawberry Perl is a common distribution. Start every script with `use strict;` and `use warnings;`: they catch typos and unsafe code.

body.code:
perl hello.pl
# Hello, world!
perl -e 'print "Hello from a one-liner\n"'

body: Statements end with a semicolon. Comments start with `#`. Double-quoted strings interpolate variables and escapes such as `\n`; single-quoted strings are literal.
Perl variables start with a sigil that shows the kind of value. Declare each variable with `my`, which makes it local to the enclosing block.

body.code:
use strict;
use warnings;

my $name  = "Perl";             # scalar: one value
my $year  = 1987;
my @langs = ("Perl", "C", "sh"); # array: ordered list
my %port  = (http => 80, https => 443);  # hash: key-value pairs

print "$name since $year\n";    # Perl since 1987
print "First: $langs[0]\n";     # First: Perl (element is a scalar, so $)
print "Count: ", scalar(@langs), "\n";   # Count: 3
print "HTTPS: $port{https}\n";  # HTTPS: 443
print "Sum: ", "10" + 5, "\n";  # Sum: 15 (strings convert to numbers)
print "Join: " . "a" . "b" x 3, "\n";    # Join: abbb

rows: scalar: a number, string or reference
array: an ordered list of scalars

body.note: Perl has separate operators for numbers and strings: `==`, `<` and `<=>` compare numbers, while `eq`, `lt` and `cmp` compare strings. Using `==` on strings such as `"abc" == "xyz"` is true (both are 0 as numbers) and prints a warning under `use warnings`.

body: Perl has `if`, `elsif`, `else`, `unless`, `while`, `until`, `for` and `foreach`. A short statement can be followed by a condition, which reads like English. `next` skips to the next iteration and `last` exits the loop.
False values are `0`, `"0"`, the empty string `""`, the empty list and `undef`. Everything else is true.
Define a function with `sub`. Arguments arrive in the special array `@_`, and the usual first line copies them into named variables. A subroutine can return a scalar or a list.
Modern Perl also supports signatures, as in `sub add($x, $y) { ... }`, enabled with `use v5.36;` or later, which also turns on `strict` and `warnings`.

Arrays and hashes come with powerful built-in functions such as `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `sort`, `map`, `grep`, `keys` and `exists`. Nested data uses references: `[ ... ]` creates an array reference and `{ ... }` a hash reference, and `->` follows them.
Inside a `sort` block, `$a` and `$b` are the two items being compared. `<=>` compares numerically and `cmp` compares as strings; plain `sort @list` sorts as strings, so `10` comes before `9`.

Regular expressions are built into Perl's syntax, which is its signature feature. `=~` applies a match `m/.../` or a substitution `s/.../.../`. Captured groups are available as `$1`, `$2` and so on, and modifiers such as `g` (global) and `i` (case-insensitive) follow the closing slash.
Use `qr/.../` to store a compiled pattern in a variable, and the `x` modifier to write long patterns over several lines with comments.

`die` raises an exception and `warn` prints a warning to standard error. `eval { ... }` catches an exception and puts the error message in `$@`. System calls such as `open` return false on failure and set `$!` to the operating system error, so check them with `or die`.

A `die` message that ends with `\n` is printed as written; without the newline, Perl appends the file name and line number. Since Perl 5.34 there is also an experimental `try`/`catch` feature, and modules such as Try::Tiny are widely used.

sections.h: A small complete program: log level counter
body: This script reads a log from files named on the command line or from standard input, counts lines by level and prints a sorted summary. It shows the diamond operator `<>`, regular expressions, hashes and `printf`.

body.code:
perl logstat.pl app.log
# 120 lines read
# INFO   97
# WARN   18
# ERROR   5

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: leaving out `use strict` and `use warnings`; using `==` for strings; forgetting `chomp` after reading a line, so the newline stays attached; confusing `$array[0]` (one element) with `@array` (the whole list); and not checking the return value of `open`.

faq.a: Yes. Perl is preinstalled on most Unix-like systems and is still common in system administration, text processing, bioinformatics and long-running business systems, although fewer new web projects start in Perl.

faq.q: What is the difference between Perl and Raku?
faq.a: Raku began as Perl 6 but became a separate language with a different design. Perl 5 continues to be developed independently, and the name Perl refers to it.

faq.q: Why do Perl variables start with $, @ and %?
faq.a: The sigil shows what kind of value you get: `$` for a single scalar, `@` for a list and `%` for a hash. That is why one element of `@items` is written `$items[0]`.

faq.q: What does chomp do in Perl?
faq.a: `chomp` removes a trailing newline from a string, which you usually need after reading a line from a file or the keyboard.

faq.q: Is Perl good for regular expressions?
faq.a: Yes. Regular expressions are part of Perl's core syntax, and PCRE, the regex library used by many other tools and languages, is named after Perl's regex style.
